content: The Pap smear, also known as the Papanicolaou test, Pap test, cervical smear, or smear test, is a medical screening procedure developed by Georgios Papanikolaou. It is primarily used to detect premalignant and malignant changes in the ectocervix. Additionally, it can identify infections and abnormalities in the endocervix and endometrium, although it is not a reliable screening tool for endometrial malignancy. During the procedure, a sample of cells is collected from the outer opening of the cervix (the os) using a device such as an Aylesbury spatula or a plastic-fronded broom. The endocervix may be partially sampled, but due to its anatomical structure, consistent and reliable sampling is not guaranteed. Abnormal endocervical cells, if present, can be identified by trained examiners. The endometrium is not directly sampled, but exfoliated cells from this region may be collected and analyzed. The Pap smear is particularly effective in detecting precancerous changes, known as dysplasias or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), which are often caused by sexually transmitted human papillomaviruses (HPVs). The test aims to identify and prevent the progression of HPV-induced cervical cancer and other abnormalities in the female genital tract. It involves staining the collected cells using the Papanicolaou technique, which highlights cytoplasmic keratinization and nuclear features for microscopic examination. The sample is then screened by a trained cytotechnologist or pathologist. The sensitivity of conventional cytology is approximately 72%, with a specificity of 94%. Liquid-based cytology, introduced in the mid-1990s, involves placing the sample in a vial containing a liquid medium (usually ethanol-based) to preserve the cells. This method has slightly different sensitivity (61–66%) and specificity (82–91%) rates compared to conventional cytology. Some studies suggest that liquid-based methods may improve sensitivity, but this is not universally observed. Abnormal Pap smear results occur in about 5–7% of cases and may indicate conditions such as dysplasia, which can range from low-grade to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL and HSIL). These abnormalities are classified using the Bethesda system, which includes categories such as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), atypical squamous cells that cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H), LSIL, HSIL, and squamous cell carcinoma. Glandular epithelial cell abnormalities, such as atypical glandular cells not otherwise specified (AGC-NOS), can also be detected. Infections, including yeast, herpes simplex virus, and Trichomonas vaginalis, may be identified, although the test is not highly sensitive for these pathogens. The Pap smear is not a perfect test. It has a false-negative rate of 15–35%, and its effectiveness depends on proper sample collection, regular screening, and appropriate follow-up of abnormal results. In the United States, over half of invasive cervical cancers occur in women who have never had a Pap smear, and an additional 10–20% occur in those who have not been screened in the preceding five years. Adenocarcinoma of the cervix, which accounts for about 15% of cervical cancers in the UK, is not effectively prevented by Pap smears. The introduction of HPV testing has improved the sensitivity of cervical cancer screening. HPV testing can detect high-risk HPV types (e.g., types 16, 18, 31, 45) that are associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cervical cancer. The sensitivity of HPV testing ranges from 88–97%, with specificity between 73–93%. Combining HPV testing with Pap smears is recommended for women over 30 years of age to enhance detection rates. Randomized controlled trials have shown that HPV testing is as sensitive as immediate colposcopy while reducing the number of unnecessary colposcopies. The Pap smear procedure involves inserting a speculum into the vagina to visualize the cervix and collect a cell sample. The test is typically not performed during menstruation. While the procedure is usually only slightly painful, factors such as patient anatomy, practitioner skill, and psychological factors can influence discomfort. Results are generally available within three weeks. Minor side effects, such as slight bleeding or cramping, may occur afterward. Other tests, such as endometrial biopsies for uterine cancer detection, can sometimes be performed during the same visit. Automation in Pap smear analysis has been developed in recent years, with computer image analysis systems improving sensitivity and reducing unsatisfactory specimens. These systems, approved by the FDA, are used in high-volume laboratories with human oversight. The Pap smear, when combined with regular screening and appropriate follow-up, can reduce cervical cancer deaths by up to 80%. However, its effectiveness is limited by factors such as irregular screening, inadequate follow-up, and sampling or interpretation errors. In the UK, the Pap smear screening program is estimated to prevent approximately 700 deaths annually, saving one life for every 15,000–20,000 women tested. Despite its limitations, the Pap smear remains a cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention, with HPV vaccination offering additional long-term benefits.
